title: Losing the bag and ten years peddling vegetables
summary: After leaving the post office he went broke, bought a truck and sold produce for about ten years.

blocks.x: Well, Uncle Sam is a tough man to work for. If you lose, I lost, I wasn't one day, I had a little bottle, a little vial, like, you know, with some kind of acid in it. Now, my bag had a corner of it, it had a hole in it about that big. Just big, large enough for me to lose it. And I caught myself putting this in there. I didn't want it on top. I didn't want it at the bottom. I knew I had to hold. So I put it in the middle. Well, as I went to the Carson, I know all the mill rooms in Chicago right now from that. I went to the mill room called Superior and Scott. And I delivered that. And I had a few more pieces of mill left. See, we used to get a whole lot of them big flats, cut the shoulder. They didn't like the mill, man. Now they got this little thing to push. We didn't have that. If you run into them magazines, they're gonna kill you, see. Sometimes you'd have two bags. So anyhow, I lost it. When I got there, I was looking for where it's gone. So then you have to double back. And first you got to look around and go back where you previously stopped. And I, which I did. So I went in and I reported that it was lost. So I have to sit down and write a statement and a second. So I put it on there. I wouldn't have lost it, but I've been asking Mr. Gross for a new bag. And I'm looking at two brand new Carl Hauer bags there and he won't give me any. So I put that in there. Well, he deleted that, you understand. He wasn't gonna have to wrap against him, you understand. So I ended up getting five days off. See what I'm talking about in so many, the mirrors. See what I'm talking about? So I quit there. And later on, that's when I, I used to see a fella there to call Wayne, one of them fella, about elevated. People was coming down around three and four o'clock. And he had three guys there, this is seven, you know. A lot of vegetables, peaches and things, you know. So I had some money. I said, well, I'm not doing anything. I saw the money go down from about $5,000. You weren't playing that long? So I'm down to about $1,700 now, you know. You weren't getting enough?

It wasn't high. What year was that in? Well, it was, it must have been in the, in the early, it was, it was after the war, because I came down here in 46. Yeah. And I must have started after 46. And so I could see I was getting broke, you know, and I started to gamble too. And so I said, well, if I don't do something soon. So I bought a truck from my uncle for $60, International, and had it fixed up. Then I started pedaling. I had a long ride. I didn't get back home until around 8, 3, 4 to 9. And I bought good stuff. See, it's all in your buying. I'd go to two markets. I'd go out to, there's the market 71st Street. Well, these guys down at the big market, that's, those are, those are the concessions, you understand? You got the front guys, front and front. So I'd catch them farmers from in there, I'd go to them mustard greens, you know, and tunnels. And then I'd shoot on over there, about 6 o'clock, and be over there. And you get some good buys. I bought turnips, boxes of turnips with 12 bunches in there for a quarter of a box. You catch a guy stuck, he's down in the basement and he got them up to the ceiling. See, they have contracts for certain grows, a certain amount of stuff every week or every month. And now if they can't get rid of that stuff in time, they're stuck, that's where you come in. Hey, Jackson, we're beginning to know you. I got a good deal for you. Come on, we went on downstairs. So I loaded up, I'd load up with a whole truckload of them greens, and I'd get me some onions, potatoes, you know, going along with it, tomatoes. And gone out, me and my load only cost me $15, $20. And sometime I'd have two boys with me, it was an alley in Chicago, I'd drop one off in this alley, drop one off in this alley. Well, I paid them $0.20 on the dollars, and they'd hustle. So I'd just stay on the corner, can't wait until they come and reload, you see. Made pretty good money.
How long did you stay with them?
